issues.description: The abstract and introduction define moral incongruence as 'the interaction of behavioral frequency and moral disapproval of a behavior,' but the methods section redefines the key predictor differently. Specifically, the methods state: 'Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.' This is a fundamentally different operationalization—severity of consequences is not the same as frequency of behavior. The rest of the paper (hypotheses, analytic plan, power analysis) consistently uses frequency, not severity of consequences, making this a direct internal contradiction that undermines the clarity of the registered design.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action. That is, the present study seeks to test whether the observed effects of interactions present in prior literature for pornography use (i.e., between moral disapproval and frequency of use) extend to addictive disorders more broadly.

issues.description: The manuscript reports inconsistent Cohen's d values for the same effect sizes. For the smallest effect, the text first states 'Cohen's d = .24' and then later in the same paragraph states 'Cohen's d = .25' for what appears to be the same study and effect (Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016). Similarly, the SESOI section references 'β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25' but earlier in the same paragraph the same study is cited with 'Cohen's d = .22' for ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016. These inconsistencies suggest transcription errors in effect size reporting and undermine confidence in the precision of the equivalence region specification.
issues.quote: Prior studies of moral incongruence have found moral incongruence to have small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)... we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)

issues.description: The relationship between reported ΔR2, f2, and Cohen's d values is internally inconsistent across multiple effect size sets. For example, ΔR2 = .072 is reported with f2 = .12 and Cohen's d = .69. However, f2 = ΔR2/(1-R2_full), so f2 = .12 would require a specific total R2 value. More critically, the conversion from f2 to Cohen's d is not straightforward and requires additional assumptions not stated. Cohen's d = .69 corresponds approximately to r ≈ .33 or R2 ≈ .11, which is inconsistent with ΔR2 = .072. These conversions appear to conflate different effect size families without appropriate justification or formula specification, making the SESOI rationale difficult to evaluate.
issues.quote: to moderate (ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12, Cohen's d = .69; Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020), to relatively large (ΔR2 = .12, f2 = .23, Cohen's d = .97, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020) effects

issues.description: The Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) as presented in the supplemental materials uses a non-standard response scale. The standard PGSI uses a 4-point scale scored 0 (never), 1 (sometimes), 2 (most of the time), 3 (almost always). However, the supplemental materials show the scale scored as Never=0, Sometimes=2, Most of the time=4, Almost Always=5. This is not the validated scoring of the PGSI. The jump from 4 to 5 (skipping an integer) and the doubling of intermediate values fundamentally alters the psychometric properties of the instrument and makes scores incomparable to the validated cutoffs (e.g., score of 8+ for problem gambling). The methods text states 'Responses will be averaged' rather than summed, which further departs from validated PGSI scoring.
issues.quote: Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)... Responses will be averaged.

issues.description: The Brief Pornography Screen (BPS) as described in the methods states responses are on 'a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often)' and that 'Responses are summed.' However, the supplemental materials show the BPS scored as Never=0, Occasionally=2, Very Often=4—a scale with values 0, 2, and 4, not 0, 1, and 2. This discrepancy between the methods description and the actual instrument means the scoring range would be 0-20 (not 0-10 as implied by the methods description), and the psychometric properties described in the validation literature (Kraus et al., 2020) may not apply to this modified scoring.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt... by reporting the frequency they have experienced certain behaviors... on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.description: The NIDA-ASSIST composite score is computed by averaging five items that use incompatible response scales. Three items use a 0-5 frequency scale, while two items ('friend/family concern' and 'failure to control') use a 0/3/6 scale. Averaging items with different ranges and distributions without standardization will produce a composite score that is dominated by the 0/3/6 items (which have larger variance) and is psychometrically unsound. The manuscript does not address this scaling incompatibility or justify the averaging approach.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest... Participants will also respond to two questions... for each substance on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months).

issues.description: The study combines a nationally representative sample (n=2,500) with a sports-wagering oversample (n=1,500) and treats them as a combined sample of N=4,000 for most analyses. However, the sports-wagering oversample is not representative of the general population and will systematically inflate gambling prevalence, gambling frequency, and potentially gambling-related moral disapproval relative to the general population. The analytic plan does not specify how these two samples will be handled in combined analyses, whether sample membership will be included as a covariate, or whether analyses will be conducted separately by sample. This design confound is particularly problematic for the gambling analyses, which are central to the study's hypotheses.
issues.quote: Due to the budgetary constraints associated with the larger grant funding effort from which this project is derived, the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age and gender. Furthermore, due to the design of the larger project from which this sample is taken, we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically.

issues.description: The study is explicitly described as a secondary analysis embedded within a larger study ('an upcoming study... funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming') whose 'primary focus is to assess the prevalence of sports-wagering behaviors.' The authors did not design the parent study, meaning they have limited control over sampling decisions, measure selection, survey order effects, and other design features. The registered report format implies prospective design control, but the actual design is constrained by a pre-existing grant and data collection protocol. This raises questions about whether the measures included are truly optimal for the stated hypotheses or are compromises imposed by the parent study's priorities.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming. The primary focus of this project is to assess the prevalence of sports-wagering behaviors in the American public.

issues.description: Gambling frequency is assessed using a single item asking about overall gambling behavior, but the methods state 'To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.' This is contradictory—the supplemental materials show only a single gambling frequency item ('Gambled or placed bets at all'), yet the methods describe averaging across multiple gambling behaviors. If only one item is used, averaging is meaningless. Furthermore, a single-item frequency measure for a heterogeneous behavior category (casino gambling, lottery, sports betting, etc.) has unknown reliability and validity, particularly when compared to the multi-item validated measures used for pornography (BPS) and gambling problems (PGSI).
issues.quote: We will assess gambling frequency using a single item... To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.description: The theoretical definition of moral incongruence requires that a person both engages in a behavior AND morally disapproves of it—the interaction captures the amplification of use-addiction links by disapproval. However, the study administers moral disapproval measures to ALL participants regardless of whether they engage in the behavior. This means the interaction term will include non-users who morally disapprove, which is conceptually incoherent (a non-user cannot experience moral incongruence about a behavior they don't engage in). While the analytic plan mentions subsetting to users for some analyses, the administration of measures to all participants and the lack of a clear, consistent rule for who is included in each moderation analysis creates construct validity problems.
issues.quote: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.

issues.description: Moral disapproval for all substances and gambling is measured with a single item ('I believe that using ________ is morally wrong'). Single-item measures have unknown reliability and cannot be assessed for internal consistency. More critically, moral disapproval is a multidimensional construct that may include personal moral beliefs, perceived social norms, religious proscriptions, and harm-based judgments. A single item cannot capture this complexity. While the pornography moral disapproval literature has used single items, extending this approach to substances and gambling without validation is a significant construct validity limitation that is not adequately acknowledged.
issues.quote: Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography. For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong' on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.description: Pornography viewing frequency is assessed with a single item measuring only solo pornography use ('Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)'). This excludes partnered pornography use, which is a common behavior. The measure therefore does not capture total pornography use frequency, creating a systematic underestimation of use for individuals who primarily or frequently view pornography with partners. This is particularly problematic given that frequency is one of the two components of the moral incongruence interaction term.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.description: The study uses validated, multi-item scales for pornography (BPS, 5 items) and gambling (PGSI, 9 items) but relies on a modified, unvalidated 5-item NIDA-ASSIST composite for all substance use outcomes. The NIDA-ASSIST items were not designed or validated as a composite addiction severity measure in the way proposed here. Furthermore, the BPS and PGSI are validated for their specific domains, while the ASSIST composite is not validated for any of the substances in this context. This non-equivalence in outcome measure quality across behaviors means that any observed differences in moral incongruence effects could be attributable to measurement differences rather than true behavioral differences, fundamentally undermining the comparative logic of the study.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, causal language is used to describe what are cross-sectional associations. The study explicitly acknowledges being cross-sectional in the limitations section, yet the hypotheses and discussion use language like 'moral incongruence predicts,' 'moral disapproval amplifies the links,' and 'moral incongruence is a clear contributor to self-reported feelings of addiction.' The limitations section notes this only briefly. Given that moral disapproval and self-reported addiction feelings could be simultaneously caused by a third variable (e.g., general negative affect, neuroticism, or religious identity), or that feeling addicted could cause increased moral disapproval (reverse causation), causal claims are not warranted.
issues.quote: Ultimately, the PPMI model implies two strong claims regarding the role of moral incongruence in predicting self-perceived feelings of addiction. The first of these claims is relatively straightforward: moral incongruence is a clear contributor to self-reported feelings of addiction to, compulsivity in, or problems with pornography use.

issues.description: The interaction between moral disapproval and use frequency as a predictor of self-reported addiction feelings may be confounded by several unaddressed variables. Most critically, negative affect and general psychological distress could independently elevate both moral disapproval (through increased self-criticism) and self-reported addiction feelings (through negative self-evaluation), creating a spurious interaction. Similarly, trait guilt-proneness or shame-proneness could drive all three variables. The study includes only religiousness, age, and gender as covariates, which is insufficient to rule out these alternative explanations. No measure of general negative affect, neuroticism, or shame/guilt-proneness is included.
issues.quote: In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates, as prior work has demonstrated clear links between such variables and self-reported problematic pornography use.

issues.description: Hypotheses 1b, 2a, and 3a predict that moral disapproval of a behavior will positively predict self-reported feelings of addiction to that behavior. This is potentially tautological: both moral disapproval and self-reported addiction feelings are negatively valenced self-evaluations of the same behavior. The manuscript acknowledges this problem in the introduction ('it is not surprising to find links between these two domains as they are both negatively valenced judgments about the same behavior') but then proceeds to include these direct effects as formal hypotheses. Testing these direct effects adds little theoretical value and may inflate the apparent support for the broader model.
issues.quote: Another plausible, if not likely, explanation is that disapproval of and distress regarding one's own behaviors are likely related to each other. More simply, it is not surprising to find links between these two domains as they are both negatively valenced judgments about the same behavior.

issues.description: The gambling frequency scale in the supplemental materials uses a 0-5 scale (Never=0, Once or Twice=1, Monthly=2, Weekly=3, Daily or Almost Daily=4, More than Once Per Day=5), but the methods text states participants will report frequency 'on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).' This is a direct numerical inconsistency between the methods description and the actual instrument. The pornography frequency scale in the supplemental materials also uses 0-5 (Never=0), while the methods describe it as '1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).' This affects how the interaction term is computed and interpreted.
issues.quote: Participants will be asked how often they have engaged in the behavior over the past 12 months using the same 6-point scale described above, ranging from 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

issues.description: The methods section states pornography viewing frequency will be assessed 'on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day),' but the supplemental materials show the scale as Never=0, Once or Twice=1, Monthly=2, Weekly=3, Daily or Almost Daily=4, More than Once Per Day=5. Additionally, the methods state 'only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months (i.e., scores > 1 on the frequency measure) will complete the remaining items,' but if never=0 (as in the supplemental), the cutoff should be scores > 0, not > 1. This inconsistency could lead to incorrect exclusion of participants who viewed pornography once or twice.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed using the same modified frequency scale as is present on the ASSIST, wherein participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)... only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months (i.e., scores > 1 on the frequency measure) will complete the remaining items

issues.description: The analytic plan states 'we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest.' However, Table 1 lists 7 target behaviors/substances (alcohol, tobacco/nicotine, cannabis/THC, prescription drug misuse, illicit drug use, pornography, gambling). The introduction and hypotheses section also lists 7 behaviors. It is unclear what the 8th analysis is, unless the authors are counting the NIDA-ASSIST pornography items and the BPS as separate analyses, but this is not clearly specified.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively).

issues.description: The hypotheses are presented without consistent numbering. The analytic plan references 'hypotheses 2b and 3b' but the hypotheses section does not use numbered labels (1a, 1b, 2a, 2b, etc.). This makes it impossible to clearly identify which specific hypothesis is being referenced in the analytic plan, creating ambiguity about which predictions correspond to which equivalence tests. This is a significant problem for a registered report, where precise pre-specification is essential.
issues.quote: Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction for moral disapproval of a behavior and frequency of that behavior fall fully within our equivalence region, we may reasonably conclude that the true effect is so low as to be null or practically null, thereby supporting hypotheses 2b and 3b, listed above.

issues.description: The study plans to conduct 8 moderation analyses (or more, given the dual outcomes for pornography and gambling) across multiple behaviors. No correction for multiple comparisons is mentioned or planned. With 8+ simultaneous hypothesis tests at α=.05, the familywise error rate is substantially elevated. The use of Holm-adjusted statistics is mentioned only for bivariate correlations, not for the primary moderation analyses. This is particularly problematic given that the study's conclusions depend on finding a significant interaction for pornography but null interactions for other behaviors—without multiple comparison correction, the pattern of results could easily arise by chance.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package... As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software, followed by equivalence tests using the reg.equiv.fd function

issues.description: The analytic plan does not specify how the nationally representative sample (n=2,500) and the sports-wagering oversample (n=1,500) will be combined or handled in analyses. There is no mention of whether sample type will be included as a covariate, whether analyses will be stratified by sample, whether sampling weights will be applied, or how the overrepresentation of gamblers will be addressed. This is a critical omission for a registered report, as the analytic decisions about sample combination will substantially affect results.
issues.quote: This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.description: The analytic plan specifies that gender will be coded as 'binary where 1 = male, and 0 = not-male.' However, no plan is provided for participants who identify as non-binary, transgender, or otherwise outside the binary. The YouGov panel data includes gender as a variable, but the coding scheme described excludes meaningful analysis of gender diversity. No justification is provided for this binary coding, and no sensitivity analysis or alternative approach is described for non-binary participants.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.description: Illicit drug use is treated as a single category with a single moral disapproval item ('I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong'). However, illicit drugs encompass an extremely heterogeneous set of substances (heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, MDMA, psychedelics, etc.) with vastly different addiction profiles, prevalence rates, and moral valences. No plan is provided for how to handle participants who use multiple illicit substances or how to interpret a single moral disapproval item for such a heterogeneous category. This aggregation likely introduces substantial measurement error.
issues.quote: I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong.

issues.description: The analytic plan states that 'focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated' in SPSS, but then states 'For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.' These two statements are contradictory—it is unclear whether variables will be mean-centered before computing the interaction term or entered in raw form. This distinction matters for interpretation of lower-order effects in the moderation model and for the equivalence testing of the interaction term.
issues.quote: focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated... For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

issues.description: Despite claiming 'we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data,' the study involves a complex survey with multiple skip patterns (e.g., only past-year users complete problematic use measures). No plan is provided for handling cases where participants skip items, provide inconsistent responses (e.g., reporting never using a substance but then endorsing urges to use it), or drop out mid-survey. The reliance on YouGov's 'proprietary data collection standards' as a complete solution to data quality is insufficient for a registered report.
issues.quote: As this data will be obtained via YouGov Opinion Polling, certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.description: The manuscript claims to use 'a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500)' but the total sample of N=4,000 includes 1,500 sports-wagering individuals who are explicitly not representative. The abstract and methods describe the study as involving 'a representative sample of the U.S. population' without adequately flagging that 37.5% of the total sample is a non-representative oversample. Conclusions drawn from the combined sample cannot be generalized to the U.S. population, and the manuscript does not consistently acknowledge this limitation.
issues.quote: This work will make use of an upcoming study (N=4,000) involving a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500).

issues.description: The study makes broad theoretical claims about whether moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior 'in addictions' generally, but the sample is limited to U.S. adults. The manuscript acknowledges that 'moral incongruence as it relates to pornography use does appear to vary somewhat by the cultural context in which it is studied,' yet the conclusions are framed as if they will resolve the general theoretical question. The U.S. context has specific cultural, religious, and legal features (e.g., varying cannabis legality, specific religious demographics) that limit generalizability of findings about moral disapproval to other populations.
issues.quote: Although a nationally representative sample in the U.S. is better than convenience sampling methods, such a sample represents only one broad cultural context in which these hypotheses could be tested.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames its findings as having implications for clinical diagnosis of CSBD and treatment-seeking populations. However, the study uses a community/population sample, and the authors themselves acknowledge that 'the effects of moral incongruence on feelings of addiction are most critical in treatment seeking populations' and that 'prevalence rates in clinical settings are largely unknown.' The leap from population-level associations to clinical diagnostic implications is not justified by the study design.
issues.quote: Should results confirm the above hypotheses, this work would have broad implications for current controversies regarding CSBD... should we find that moral incongruence—defined as the interaction between moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior—only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model.

issues.description: The study is explicitly framed as seeking to 'demonstrate that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors' and to provide 'strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI.' This confirmatory framing in a registered report is problematic because it reveals a strong prior commitment to one outcome. The hypotheses are structured so that confirming the authors' preferred theory (moral incongruence is unique to pornography) is the primary goal, while disconfirmation is treated as a secondary, less likely outcome. This framing may introduce subtle analytic flexibility in how results are interpreted, particularly in the exploratory fallback analyses.
issues.quote: Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior, in contrast with other addictions.

issues.description: The SESOI of δ=|.11| is described as 'extremely conservative' because it is based on the smallest observed effect in prior pornography literature. However, using the smallest observed pornography effect as the equivalence bound for non-pornography behaviors is logically circular: it assumes that any effect smaller than the smallest pornography effect is practically null for other behaviors. This reasoning does not account for the possibility that moral incongruence effects for substances or gambling might be real and meaningful but simply smaller than for pornography. The equivalence test as designed can only show that effects are smaller than the pornography benchmark, not that they are truly null.
issues.quote: Collectively, then, setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision. However, as a primary purpose of the present work is to evaluate whether moral incongruence is unique in its contribution to self-reports of pornography addiction, in contrast to other addictions, we elected to use an especially small SESOI for our analyses.

issues.description: The study uses standard significance testing (NHST) to confirm the pornography moral incongruence hypothesis (H1) but uses equivalence testing to support null hypotheses for gambling and substances (H2b, H3b). This asymmetric framework means the pornography hypothesis benefits from the low bar of p<.05 while the null hypotheses for other behaviors require passing a more stringent equivalence test. A more rigorous approach would use equivalence testing or Bayesian methods consistently across all hypotheses, or would pre-specify a minimum effect size that would count as confirmation for the pornography hypothesis as well.
issues.quote: Consistent with prior studies, we expect to find that moral incongruence regarding pornography use will predict self-reported feelings of addiction... We expect to find that moral incongruence as it relates to gambling behaviors, will not predict self-reported levels of gambling disorder symptoms... we anticipate that equivalence tests will reveal the effect of this interaction to fall within the equivalence interval

issues.description: The analytic plan includes multiple fallback or exploratory analyses that are triggered by specific outcomes (e.g., if equivalence tests fail, redefine the equivalence region using the lower bound of the 95% CI for the pornography interaction). These conditional analyses introduce researcher degrees of freedom because the decision to use them depends on the observed data. While pre-registering these contingencies is better than not pre-registering them, the cascading conditional structure (primary SESOI → fallback using pornography CI lower bound → further exploratory analyses) creates a garden of forking paths that could be navigated post-hoc to support preferred conclusions.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.description: The analytic plan states that if regression assumptions are 'substantially violated,' supplemental analyses will be conducted, and if results 'remain robust,' OLS results will be presented in text. However, 'substantially violated' and 'remain robust' are not operationally defined. The criteria for deciding when a violation is substantial enough to warrant supplemental analysis, and when results are robust enough to present OLS as primary, are left to post-hoc researcher judgment. This creates undisclosed flexibility in the primary analysis pipeline.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate. Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results and corresponding graphs in text

issues.description: The analytic plan states that 'for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample' based on past-year engagement in each behavior. However, the specific inclusion criteria for each subsample are not fully pre-specified. For example, it is unclear whether participants who report 'once or twice' in the past year are included as 'users' for the moderation analysis, or only those with more frequent use. The threshold for inclusion in each behavior-specific analysis is not operationally defined in the analytic plan, leaving this decision to post-hoc judgment.
issues.quote: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior... for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample.

issues.description: The manuscript states 'we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data' based solely on YouGov's proprietary quality control. This is an unrealistic assumption for a survey covering sensitive topics (substance use, pornography, gambling, moral beliefs) with complex skip patterns. Even with panel data, item-level missingness, skip logic errors, and partial completions are common. No plan for handling missing data (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation, full information maximum likelihood) is provided. For a registered report, this omission is particularly problematic as it leaves missing data handling entirely unspecified.
issues.quote: Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.description: The study design includes skip patterns where only past-year users complete problematic use and moral disapproval measures. This creates systematic missingness that is not random—non-users who are excluded from analyses may differ systematically from users on key variables (e.g., religiousness, age, gender). The analytic plan does not address whether the restriction to users introduces selection bias into the moderation analyses, nor does it consider whether the pattern of who uses each substance/behavior is itself informative for the moral incongruence hypotheses.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

issues.description: The study is funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming, an organization with a specific interest in gambling research and responsible gaming. The study includes gambling as a key comparison behavior and hypothesizes that moral incongruence will NOT predict gambling disorder symptoms. A finding that moral incongruence does not inflate gambling disorder self-reports (unlike pornography) could be interpreted as supporting the validity of gambling disorder diagnoses and potentially the gambling industry's interest in framing gambling problems as genuine disorders rather than moral judgments. This potential conflict of interest is not disclosed or discussed in the manuscript.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming.

issues.description: The study embeds its measures within a larger survey on sports wagering. The order in which measures are presented to participants is not specified, and no plan for counterbalancing or controlling for order effects is described. Given that the survey covers sensitive topics (pornography, substance use, gambling, moral beliefs), the order of presentation could substantially affect responses through priming, demand characteristics, or fatigue effects. This is particularly relevant for moral disapproval items, which may be influenced by prior questions about behavior frequency.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming. The primary focus of this project is to assess the prevalence of sports-wagering behaviors in the American public.

issues.description: The study makes multiple modifications to the validated NIDA-ASSIST instrument: adding pornography and gambling as response options, modifying the response scale by adding a 'more than once per day' category, and computing a composite score by averaging items with incompatible scales. The authors acknowledge that 'such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography' but claim this 'will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.' This claim is unsubstantiated. Modifying a validated instrument without revalidation means the psychometric properties (reliability, validity, factor structure) of the modified version are unknown.
issues.quote: We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST, in addition to the measures listed above... Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.description: The methods describe a complex approach to alcohol frequency measurement: the NIDA Quick Screen asks about heavy episodic drinking (5+ drinks for men, 4+ for women), but the authors state they will 'look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).' The supplemental materials show a general alcohol frequency item. However, the gender-specific heavy drinking items are also included in the supplemental materials as separate questions. The analytic plan does not specify which alcohol frequency measure will be used in the moderation analysis, creating ambiguity about the primary predictor.
issues.quote: In its original form, the NIDA Quick Screen asks men to report alcohol frequency in terms of how many days they have consumed five or more drinks in a day and women to report alcohol frequency in terms of days they have consumed four or more drinks per day. Although we will include these response options, for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally.

issues.description: The manuscript conflates religiousness and moral disapproval throughout, sometimes treating them as interchangeable proxies for moral incongruence.
